Incident Command Runbook and Escalation Matrix

Summary
-------
This runbook defines the incident command structure, escalation matrix, triage playbooks, on-call rotation norms, game day checklist, and customer/status communications templates for production incidents that affect Redwood Inference hosted and dedicated inference services. It is written for responders (SRE, Platform, Serving Runtime, and Product engineers) and on-call leads.

Purpose
-------
- Provide a single-source-of-truth for running incidents from detection to postmortem.
- Ensure incidents are handled predictably with clear ownership, SLA-aware decisions, and consistent external comms.
- Reduce time-to-detect and time-to-recover by standardizing diagnostic steps and escalation paths.

Scope
-----
This document covers:
- Severity definition and SLO thresholds for public-facing inference endpoints (hosted API and dedicated endpoints).
- Incident command roles & responsibilities.
- Escalation matrix for common failure modes.
- Runbooks for high-frequency incident classes (latency spikes, 5xx error surge, GPU node OOM, KV cache corruption, control-plane auth failures).
- On-call rotation conventions, handoff checklist, and paging policy.
- Game day exercises and postmortem timeline.
- Standard status page and customer email templates.

Definitions and Severity Tiers
----------------------------
- Severity P0 (Critical): Service unavailable for >5% of customer traffic or complete loss of model-serving in a region; severe data-loss risk. Target TTR (time to restore): 60 minutes.
- Severity P1 (High): Significant degradation (latency above SLO for >20% traffic, or sustained 5xx rate >2%). Target TTR: 4 hours.
- Severity P2 (Medium): Minor degradation, single-service feature broken, limited scope. Target TTR: 24 hours.
- Severity P3 (Low): Cosmetic issues, docs, or non-urgent config changes.

SLOs and Alert Thresholds
------------------------
Primary SLOs (production, per-region):
- Availability: 99.95% successful requests (5xx excluded) per 30d window.
- Latency: 95th percentile token-generation latency < 450ms for small models (<=1B), < 800ms for mid models (1B-10B) measured on redwood-serve-prod across business hours.
- Error budget burn alerts: 25%/50%/100% burn in 7d window triggers paging to SRE lead.

Alert examples and thresholds:
- high-5xx-rate: firing if 5xx_rate > 0.02 for 5m for router-api (pager: PD:Infra-Production).
- slow-p95-latency: p95(latency) > 800ms for 10m for model-router (pager: PD:Serving).
- infra-instance-down: >3 GPU nodes unreachable in pool redwood-dedicated-eu-west (pager: PD:Capacity).

Incident Command Structure
-------------------------
1) Incident Commander (IC) — role: drive resolution, decisions, and timeline. Typically the on-call SRE for the impacted service. Authority to execute rollbacks and mitigation.
2) Communications Lead (Comms) — role: writes status page updates, posts to #incidents and customer Slack/Support. Owns external comms cadence.
3) Technical Lead (TL) — role: leads deep debugging and approves remediation plan (can be same person as IC if headcount limited).
4) Triage Engineers — role: follow runbook steps, collect evidence, apply mitigations.
5) Postmortem Author — role: write the postmortem within 72 hours and track corrective actions.

Activation checklist (first 10 minutes)
------------------------------------
1. Pager triggers — acknowledge within 3 minutes.
2. IC confirms severity and opens incident in Incident Manager (Slack channel: #incident-<INC-ID>).
3. IC assigns Comms, TL, and two triage engineers.
4. Comms publishes initial status page entry (see templates).
5. Begin evidence collection: attach logs, traces, and sampling of affected request IDs.

Escalation Matrix (quick reference)
---------------------------------
- If alert is high-5xx-rate on router-api:
  - 0-5m: On-call infra SRE (PD:Infra-Production).
  - 5-20m: If unresolved, escalate to Serving on-call (PD:Serving) and add TL.
  - 20-60m: If still unresolved and customer-impacting, escalate to Eng Manager and notify Sales/Customer Success.

- If dedicated GPU pool reports node losses:
  - 0-10m: Capacity on-call (PD:Capacity).
  - 10-30m: If >3 nodes affected, engage Cloud Ops (GCP/AWS account owner) and begin capacity reroute.

- If authentication/control-plane failures (authz/authn errors for control plane):
  - Immediately page Security on-call (PD:Security) and Eng Manager. Treat as P0 until proven otherwise.

Detailed Runbooks (by incident class)
------------------------------------
A) 5xx spike on /v1/generate (router-api)
- Symptoms: sudden increase in 5xx rate, request IDs show Code=503 or Code=502.
- Immediate checks (IC or triage engineer):
  1. Grafana dashboards: router-api 5xx rate, upstream model-router 5xx, redis-kv errors.
  2. kubectl get pods -n prod | grep router-api && kubectl describe pod <pod> for OOMKills.
  3. Check model-router logs for OOMs or traceback: 
```
# example diagnostics
kubectl -n prod logs deploy/router-api -c router | tail -n 200
kubectl -n prod exec -it deploy/router-api -- /bin/sh -c 'curl -sS http://model-router:8080/health'
```
- Short-term mitigations:
  - Remove unhealthy router-api pods from load balancer: kubectl scale deployment/router-api --replicas=<healthy_count>.
  - If traffic surge from a single customer key, apply token-based rate limit via rate-limiter service: POST /admin/limits.
  - If upstream model instance failing, switch traffic to fallback model variant: update route in model-router: POST /v1/route-fallback {"model":"gpt-j-small-fallback"}.
- Post-incident action: root-cause analysis in postmortem, add synthetic test covering failing path.

B) GPU node OOM / model-worker crash (serving runtime)
- Symptoms: Node-level OOM logs, model-worker restarting, KV cache warm-up failures.
- Diagnostics:
  - gcloud compute instances list --filter='name~"redwood-gpu"' && gcloud compute ssh <instance> -- sudo journalctl -u model-worker -n 200
  - Check NVIDIA metrics: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,memory.free --format=csv -l 1
- Mitigation steps:
  1. Evacuate best-effort: cordon node and drain model workloads: kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data.
  2. If autoscaling is enabled, trigger immediate scale-up: POST to autoscaler API /admin/scale with reason="OOM incident".
  3. If memory growth suspected: roll back last config that changed batch sizes or kv cache limits (see config registry entry: configs/model-worker/batch-size).
- Recovery verification:
  - Confirm model-worker pods reach READY=1 and p95 latency returns to baseline.

C) KV prefix mismatch / cache corruption
- Symptoms: Incorrect responses, cache-miss spikes, key-not-found errors in logs.
- Diagnostics:
  - Check kv-cache metrics and last successful sync timestamp.
  - Run verification tool: curl -sS http://kv-cache:8080/verify-prefixes
- Mitigations:
  - If corruption detected, fail open to bypass cache: toggle flag in feature-flags service (feature.kv.fail_open=true).
  - Rebuild cache in background using snapshot: POST /kv-cache/rebuild?from=snapshot-YYYYMMDD.
- Post-incident action: improve snapshot frequency and add end-to-end tests.

D) Control-plane authz/authn failures
- Symptoms: Customers receiving 401/403 on login or api-key validation fail.
- Immediate actions:
  1. Page Security on-call and Engineering manager.
  2. Check Auth service status: kubectl -n controlplane get pods auth-service && curl -sS https://auth.redwood.internal/health
  3. If tokens are expired due to cert rotation, rollback rotation or re-issue certs via KMS integration.
- Communications: Comms must treat as P0 and issue status updates every 30 minutes until recovery.

On-call rotations and Handoff
---------------------------
- Rotation cadence: primary on-call rotates weekly for infra and serving teams. Secondary rotates bi-weekly.
- Handoff template (to be posted in #oncall-handoffs):
  - Time window covered: <YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM> -> <YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM>
  - Current open incidents (ID, priority, short status)
  - Known noisy alerts / silenced alerts and why
  - Temporary mitigations in place
  - Contact list for escalation (names + PagerDuty IDs)
- Handoff verification: incoming on-call must acknowledge handoff and confirm access to GCP/AWS, PagerDuty, and Slack.

Paging policy and noise reduction
-------------------------------
- Only page on-call for alerts that map to our SLO definitions. Non-SLO alerts go to Slack #alerts for triage.
- All automated alerts must include playbook links and runbook steps in the alert message.

Game Day Exercises
------------------
Cadence and objectives:
- Quarterly game days per team (Eng-SRE + Serving + Platform). One cross-team large-scale scenario annually.
- Objectives: validate runbook accuracy, verify cross-team escalation, test status page and external comms.
- Game day checklist (pre-exercise):
  1. Create synthetic incident (test alert) with clear start time and scope.
  2. Ensure test does not affect production traffic — use canary/test cluster.
  3. Observe detection -> resolution time and checklist adherence.
- Post-game-day: write game-day report, update runbooks within 5 business days.

Postmortem Requirements and Timeline
----------------------------------
- Timeline:
  - 24 hours: Incident Commander posts preliminary incident summary and assigns Postmortem Author.
  - 72 hours: Draft postmortem submitted.
  - 7 days: Postmortem reviewed and corrective actions assigned with owners and deadlines.
  - 30 days: Verify completion of corrective actions and update postmortem status.
- Postmortem template (mandatory fields):

Status Page and Customer Communications

Use status.redwood.ai for public customer-facing updates and /internal/status for customer success. Comms cadence: initial update within 15 minutes for P0/P1; status updates every 30 minutes until mitigation, hourly during recovery, and final summary when resolved.

and how to safely intervene.\n\nGoals and scope:\n- Keep 99th percentile token latency below SLO targets per tier (see SLO table).\n- Maintain per-node GPU utilization in the operational band to avoid thermal or NVLink contention (recommended 60–85% during normal traffic).\n- Limit regression risk by constraining automated changes behind safe guardrails and staged rollouts.\n- Cover both automated autotune flows and manual operator interventions.\n\nQuick reference SLOs and thresholds:\n| SLO / Metric | Target | Operator alert threshold | Action level |\n|--------------|--------|--------------------------|--------------|\n| 99p token latency (hosted-prod) | <= 120ms | >= 140ms for 5m | P1 |\n| 99p token latency (dedicated) | <= 80ms | >= 100ms for 5m | P1 |\n| GPU thermal throttle events / node | 0 per 1h | > 3 in 10m | P1 |\n| GPU memory fragmentation ratio | < 0.25 | > 0.4 | P2 |\n| Scheduler change fail rate (canary) | < 1% | > 2% | P2 |\n\nKey concepts:\n- Feedback loop inputs: aggregated traces (99p latency), kernel queue lengths, per-shard KV cache hit rates, sequence length distribution, per-GPU occupancy, and admission controller reject rates.\n- Controller outputs: kernel slot allocations, batch slicing targets, priority weight adjustments, per-tenant quota limits, and hint signals for KV cache prefetch.\n- Guardrails: change rate limit (max 5% of slots per minute), rollback window (10 minutes), and canary sampling (5% traffic by default).\n\nRoles and ownership:\n- Runtime Scheduling Team: primary owners for the feedback controller and policy language.\n- SRE on-call: monitors alerts and executes runbook actions.\n- Release lead: approves non-automated policy changes and coordinates canaries.\n- Observability team: owns metric definitions and dashboards used by the loop.\n\nAutomated feedback path (high level):\n1. Signal ingestion: streaming metrics from the collector (grpc-traces, kernel-metrics-pipeline).\n2. Signal enrichment: causal attribution service enriches latency spikes with kernel and tenant context.\n3. Decision engine: policy engine evaluates rules and candidate adjustments.\n4. Safety checks: simulated dry-run against the simulator and quota check.\n5. Apply: change is committed to the scheduler with a versioned change id and canary rollout.\n\nSafety and simulation:\n- All automated changes are run through the local decision simulator. The simulator must flag potential >3% expected 99p latency regressions or >5% drop in throughput.\n- Canary matrix: default is 5% traffic for 10 minutes, 20% for 20 minutes, then full roll. The decision engine will abort if any stage shows alert violations.\n\nOperator runbook: incident triage and mitigation steps:\n1. Confirm the alert: check 99p latency, kernel queue backlogs, and recent scheduler change IDs. CLI: redwoodctl metrics query --range 10m --metric 99p_token_latency --service serving-runtime\n2. Identify correlated signals: correlate with deployment events, kernel rollout flags, or thermal events. Use dashboard: Serving Runtime / Scheduling Feedback Loop / Recent Decisions.\n3. If automated change is in progress and latency regressed:\n   a. Rollback automated change: redwoodctl scheduler rollback --change-id <id> --reason \"latency-regression-rollback\"\n   b. Pause auto-rollouts: redwoodctl scheduler set-guardrail --auto-rollout false\n   c. Open an incident and tag the runtime-scheduling Slack channel (#runtime-scheduling) and page SRE.\n4. If no automated changes present, apply manual mitigation: reduce admission controller concurrency for affected model variant(s). Example:\n   a. redwoodctl admission update --route /v1/generate --concurrency 8\n   b. Expand canary to divert to fallback model variant if available: redwoodctl routing set-fallback --route /v1/generate --variant small-llm-quant --weight 0.25\n5. Observe for 10 minutes, collect traces: redwoodctl traces fetch --filter \"change_id:<id>\" --out /tmp/traces.json\n6. Hosted API SLO: Overload Exceptions and Error Budget Policy
STATUS: published
## Purpose
This page defines how *overload-induced* failures are categorized for Hosted API SLO measurement, how they impact error budgets, and how we communicate the impact (internally and externally). It aligns SRE, Product, Support, and Engineering on what “counts” vs what is classified separately.

This policy applies to the **Hosted API** (multi-tenant) request path, including gateway admission control, Smart Routing fallback, and serving runtime backpressure.

---

## Summary (what counts)
**Overload errors are user-visible failures and count against the Hosted API availability SLO for paid Hosted tiers.**

We additionally:
- Classify overload separately from generic 5xx to improve reporting and to ensure controlled degradation is preferred over timeouts.
- Track an internal “overload share” guardrail to prevent normalizing load shedding as steady-state behavior.
- Treat *customer-configured* rate limits and quota enforcement differently from platform overload.

---
--
## Definitions
### Overload vs rate limiting (important distinction)
- **Rate limit / quota enforcement (customer- or plan-based):** The customer exceeded a documented limit (RPM/TPM, concurrency, credits, or plan quota). This is a *contracted behavior*, not a platform incident.
- **Platform overload (capacity/dependency saturation):** Redwood rejects or degrades traffic to protect fleet health (queue depth, token/sec saturation, memory pressure, regional capacity, downstream brownout). This is a platform-side reliability event.

--
- Retry guidance (e.g., `Retry-After` when safe/appropriate)

If these are missing, SRE will classify as “generic failure” for incident reporting until corrected.

---

## Hosted API Availability SLO (current)
**Metric name (conceptual):** Hosted API Request Success Rate

**Objective:** 99.9% monthly availability (rolling 30 days) for paid Hosted tiers, measured at the API gateway.

**In-scope endpoints:**
- `/v1/chat/completions`
- `/v1/completions`
--
- `/v1/rerank`

**In-scope regions:** All public Hosted regions (reported per-region and globally).

**Notes on streaming:** For streaming responses, we treat a request as successful if we return an HTTP 200 and complete the stream without server-side termination. Server-terminated streams are failures (typically mapped to a 5xx or explicit overload code, depending on cause).
--
---

## Request classification for SLO accounting
SLO accounting happens at the gateway and is based on HTTP status, Redwood error code, and selected gateway/runtime termination reasons.

### Denominator (what is measured)
Requests are included in the availability denominator when:
- They reach the gateway and are identified as a Hosted API request, and
- Authentication is attempted (i.e., we can attribute to a tenant/project), and
- The request targets an in-scope endpoint.

### Exclusions (not counted against availability)
--
- **All 5xx**, including 500/502/503/504
- **429 with error code in the `OVERLOAD_*` family**
- **408/504** timeouts (gateway or upstream)
- **499 (client canceled)** is tracked but does not count against availability by default; it may be reclassified during incident analysis if correlated with server-side stalls.

---

## Error taxonomy mapping (SLO classes)
This table standardizes the mapping used by SRE dashboards, SLO tooling, and incident review.

| HTTP | Redwood error code (examples) | Class | SLO impact | Notes |
|------|------------------------------|-------|------------|-------|
| 2xx  | n/a | Success | Good | Includes successful streaming completion |
| 400/422 | `INVALID_REQUEST` | Client error | Excluded | Track for DX quality |
| 401/403 | `UNAUTHORIZED` / `FORBIDDEN` | Client error | Excluded | Track separately |
| 429 | `RATE_LIMITED` | Plan enforcement | Excluded | Customer exceeded documented per-tenant limit |
| 429 | `QUOTA_EXCEEDED` | Plan enforcement | Excluded | Billing/credits/quota exhausted |
| 429 | `OVERLOAD_ADMISSION_REJECTED` | Overload | Failure | Gateway admission control (concurrency/token bucket) |
| 503 | `OVERLOAD_CIRCUIT_OPEN` | Overload | Failure | Circuit breaker open at gateway/routing/runtime |
| 503 | `OVERLOAD_DOWNSTREAM_UNHEALTHY` | Overload | Failure | Dependency brownout; rejected to avoid retries/timeouts |
| 503 | `OVERLOAD_REGIONAL_CAPACITY` | Overload | Failure | Regional capacity saturation signal |
| 504 | `GATEWAY_TIMEOUT` | Timeout | Failure | Prefer converting to explicit overload when saturation-driven |
| 5xx | `INTERNAL_ERROR` | Server error | Failure | Non-overload server failures |

--
---

## Overload policy: how it impacts the error budget
### 1) Overload counts against availability (paid Hosted tiers)
Overload is a platform-side rejection and is user-visible. For paid Hosted tiers, overload responses (429/503 with `OVERLOAD_*` codes) are counted as availability failures.

Rationale:
- Customers experience a failed request regardless of “controlled” vs “uncontrolled” failure.
- Counting overload keeps incentives aligned: we must invest in capacity, routing, and dependency resilience.

--

### 3) Guardrail: “overload share” must not become steady state
In addition to the availability SLO, SRE tracks an internal guardrail:
- **Overload share (rolling 30d) target:** < 0.05% of in-scope requests globally
- **Page-worthy threshold (per-region):** sustained overload share > 0.20% for 15 minutes for any paid tier cohort

These guardrails are not contractual SLOs, but they are used for alerting and release gates.

### 4) Rate limiting and quota enforcement do not burn error budget
- `RATE_LIMITED` and `QUOTA_EXCEEDED` are excluded from availability.
- They are reported as “enforcement events” with separate dashboards.

Important: If enforcement is triggered erroneously due to platform bugs/misconfig (e.g., incorrect tier policy pushed), we treat it as an incident and may choose to reclassify for post-incident customer reporting.

---
--
- Use stable error codes so clients can implement deterministic backoff.

### Customer retry amplification (internal analysis)
For internal incident analysis, we tag overload incidents with a “retry amplification factor” estimate:
- **Amplification factor > 2.0** (requests received vs unique client operations) indicates potential retry storm.

This does *not* change SLO accounting automatically. However, for enterprise escalations and RCAs we may include a note when customer retry behavior significantly increased blast radius.

---
--
## Reporting policy
### Internal reporting (weekly + monthly)
SRE’s monthly reliability review for Hosted API must include:
- Availability (global + by region)
- Failure breakdown: overload vs timeout vs generic 5xx
--
- Top affected models/routes/tiers (bounded cardinality; do not publish raw tenant names outside restricted dashboards)

### Customer-facing reporting (status page + incidents)
When overload materially affects customers:
- Status page should describe it as **“elevated overload rejections (429/503) to protect system health”** rather than “timeouts.”
- Include impacted region(s), endpoints, and start/stop times.
--
---

## Customer tiers and SLO/SLA notes
This page governs the **platform SLO measurement**. Contractual SLAs may differ.

- **Self-serve Hosted (no SLA):** We still compute availability, but customer communications should avoid implying SLA credits.
- **Enterprise Hosted (SLA-backed):** Overload failures count toward availability for SLA measurement unless explicitly carved out in the contract.
- **Dedicated capacity:** Not covered here (separate SLO/SLA documents apply).

If a customer has a contract clause that treats certain overload events differently, Support/CS must route through SRE + Legal for interpretation before making commitments.

---
--
## Implementation requirements (for engineering teams)
To make this policy measurable and enforceable:
- Gateway must emit classification labels for all responses:
  - `availability_class = success|client_excluded|enforcement_excluded|overload_failure|timeout_failure|server_failure`
- Overload responses must include:
--
  - `x-redwood-request-id`
  - `Retry-After` where applicable
- Routing/runtime components must propagate termination reasons to gateway with bounded cardinality.

---
--
## Change management
Any changes to:
- Which statuses/codes are excluded from SLO,
- The overload guardrail thresholds,
- The definition of streaming success,
--
…require:
1) An ADR update or addendum (Architecture & Standards),
2) SRE review (owner: Rafael Mendes),
3) Product sign-off for customer-facing impact (owner: Nikhil Sharma).

---

### Example: platform overload (counts against availability)
- HTTP 503
--

## Appendix B: Open questions / follow-ups
- Evaluate whether to publish a “controlled overload rate” chart to enterprise customers during canary/GA rollout (Product + SRE).
- Confirm whether 499 reclassification is needed for known client libraries that cancel on server stalls (SDK team + SRE).

Service stability acceptance and capacity fingerprint guidelines
STATUS: published
Summary:
This guideline describes the "stability fingerprint" concept and the acceptance gates teams must pass before a new service, model variant, or major feature is promoted to production. The stability fingerprint is a compact, observable snapshot of service health and capacity behavior that drives SLO admission, capacity reservations, and automated runbook wiring.

Scope:
- Applies to all public-facing inference services and model tenants (hosted, dedicated, private control-plane integrations).
- Intended for SREs, service owners, and release engineers who approve production rollouts.

Goals:
- Provide a repeatable, machine-verifiable signal for "ready for production" across performance, cost, and reliability axes.
- Reduce post-launch firefighting by catching capacity and tail-latency failure modes during pre-production validation.
- Standardize artifact format so automated tooling (telemetry checks, CI gates, runbook wiring) can consume fingerprints.

Key definitions:
1) Stability fingerprint: a time-windowed summary of telemetry and derived signals produced by a preflight harness. The fingerprint includes quantiles, headroom margins, failure-mode counters, and workload shape descriptors.
2) Admission gate: a set of pass/fail checks (SLOs, headroom, queue-depth recovery) that must succeed for a rollout to proceed.
3) Fingerprint profile: a named baseline for a class of services (e.g., small-text-gen, chat-multiturn, embeddings-batch) used to apply tailored thresholds.

Fingerprint fields (table):
| field | description | format | example |
|---|---|---:|---|
| fingerprint_id | stable artifact id for the run | string | fp-20240715-01 |
| service | logical service name | string | inference-text-gen |
| profile | fingerprint profile name | string | chat-multiturn |
| window | measurement window | string | 10m |
| p50,p90,p95,p99 | latency quantiles (ms) | numbers | 12, 40, 80, 320 |
--
| degraded_signals | list of short tags for observed anomalies | list | ["tail-latency-spike","kv-warmup"] |

Fingerprint generation procedure (preflight harness):
1) Select the canonical traffic shape to run (profile). Include at least: steady-state ramp, microbursts, and cold-key cache stress.
2) Deploy the candidate into an isolated canary cluster with identical scheduling/quantization configs as target prod.
--
4) Run a 10–30 minute measurements window capturing latency quantiles, device counters, queue depths, error classes, and token throughput.
5) Compute derived metrics: headroom_tokens, workload_entropy, queued-request tail mass, and recovery-time-from-overload (seconds to p95 reclaim).
6) Emit fingerprint artifact (JSON or YAML) and store in the artifacts registry with artifact metadata (git commit, model id, infra config).
7) Trigger automated admission checks (see Admission gates).

Admission gates (automated checks — pass/fail):
- SLO compliance (synthetic): p95 <= profile.p95_threshold and error_rate_5xx < profile.error_threshold.
- Tail-resilience: p99/p95 ratio < profile.tail_ratio_limit.
- Headroom: headroom_tokens >= profile.min_headroom_tokens.
--
- Known-faults: degraded_signals must not contain any of the blocked list ["oom","memory-leak","kv-eviction-flood"].

If any gate fails the system returns a blocking validation error with the failing metric(s). Failures produce a Runbook wiring ticket with suggested mitigations.

SLO mapping and cost tradeoffs:
- Each profile contains a prioritized SLO set: latency (p95/p99), availability (percent of successful responses), and quality acceptance (for model changes, from eval harness).
- For low-latency profiles we allow reduced headroom but require stricter tail-resilience thresholds. For cost-sensitive profiles we accept tighter utilization ceilings but require longer stress windows to validate recovery.

Runbook wiring (automated):
- On a fingerprint failure the harness creates a runbook ticket with: summary, fingerprint_id, failing metrics, evidence links (traces, flamegraphs, heatmaps), suggested mitigations, owner team, and rollback recommendation.
- Suggested mitigations are templated: increase reserved capacity by X tokens/sec, enable the KV pre-warm flag, revert quantization change, or run a controlled scaling test.
- If a release is blocked, the runbook links to the release PR and locks the promotion pipeline until triage marks a fix.
--

Preflight CLI examples (internal tooling):
- Generate fingerprint: infra-fingerprint generate --service inference-text-gen --profile chat-multiturn --window 10m --output fp.json
- Submit for gate: infra-fingerprint submit --artifact fp.json --pipeline pr-1234
- Query artifact: infra-fingerprint list --service inference-text-gen --since 2024-07-01

Acceptance checklist (manual review items):
1) Security & secrets: credentials and KMS policies verified for the deployment.

Regional Readiness Orchestrator + Fallback Variant Selector
STATUS: In Progress
Summary:
Design and implement a Regional Readiness Orchestrator (RRO) that drives smart region selection, tier-aware routing, and fallback model-variant selection during multi-region failover. The goal is to provide predictable cutovers with minimal latency/backpressure, preserve cached state where possible, and ensure customer workloads remain within SLOs during incidents and planned maintenance.

Goals:
- Produce an orchestration service that computes a readiness score per region+tier+model-variant in real time. Scores should incorporate health probes, capacity headroom, KV/prefix cache priming status, model warmup percentiles, and recent error/latency trends.
- Route by policy: primary->tiered fallbacks->regional priority list->model variant fallback, with pluggable policies per customer/route.
- Provide gating and quorum checks before warm-standby activation to avoid noisy cutovers.
- Support graceful pre-warming of KV/prefix caches and model weights in target regions using shadow traffic and staged priming.
--

Design notes / architecture:
- Readiness scoring: combine signal inputs into a 0-100 score. Inputs include: health probe pass rate (last 1m), p90 latency delta vs baseline, GPU utilization headroom, available concurrency slots, KV-cache hit ratio and priming completeness, model-variant warmup percentile (token throughput), recent error-rate slope, and active maintenance flags. Weights are tunable per-customer.
- Orchestrator responsibilities: maintain regional inventories, compute scores, emit routing directives to the Smart Router, run preflight priming jobs (i.e., shadow requests to populate KV/prefix cache and lazy weight load), and execute cutover playbooks with stepwise traffic shifts.
- Tier routing: traffic should prefer same-tier capacity (e.g., enterprise-dedicated -> enterprise-dedicated fallback) before falling back to lower tiers. Each tier has a mapping to compatible model-variants to preserve behavior.
- Fallback model variants: model graph must be annotated with fallback relationships (e.g., standard->quantized-int8->smaller-llamax). The selector should consider compatibility of tokens, function-calling contracts, and output distribution drift risk.
- Priming strategy: stage I: control-plane scheduled prefix KV seeding for top N customers; stage II: shadow traffic at 1-5% to validate latency and output; stage III: ramp readiness gating once cache hit ratio and warmup throughput thresholds are met.
- Quorum gating: require N healthy nodes in the target region per model-variant + cache primed at >=80% + failover score delta above threshold for at least T seconds. Quorum parameters are tunable per region and per release.
- Rollback: automated rollback if error rate spikes > 2x baseline in the first 3 minutes after cutover or if p95 latency exceeds SLO by > 20% for more than 30s.

Observability and metrics:
- New metrics: region_readiness_score{region,tier,model_variant}, priming_progress{region,customer}, kv_cache_hit_ratio{region,customer}, model_warmup_tokens/sec, region_activation_events, fallback_selector_decisions.
- Dashboards: per-route readiness timeline, priming task history, recent fallbacks and reason tree, cost delta during priming.
- Alerts: readiness degradation per region, priming failures >3 attempts, activation rollback triggered.

Operational playbooks (high-level):
1) Preflight: run readiness checks for planned maintenance; operator can schedule priming window.
2) Automated warm failover: orchestrator evaluates scores, performs staged priming, executes stepwise traffic shifting and validates metrics at each step.
3) Emergency cutover: if primary region fails, orchestrator will select highest-scoring compatible region+tier and activate with conservative traffic caps then follow fast validation.
4) Postmortem: orchestrator exports decision rationale and metric traces to Console and links to incident ticket.

Security and compliance considerations:
- Priming uses customer prefixes and may touch cached customer data; must obey data residency rules and only prime within permitted regions.
- All priming requests must be labeled and logged; KMS usage for model artifacts remains enforced.

Acceptance criteria:
- RRO running in canary region and producing readiness_score metric for 3 model families.
- Smart Router respects directives for traffic shifts in canary test and fails safe to previous routing on rollback conditions.
- KV/prefix priming task can complete for a 10k prefix sample within configured window and reflect in priming_progress metric.
- Console exposes per-route operator controls and a visualization of readiness score and priming status.

Artifacts / links:
- Design doc (Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/MR/Regional+Readiness+Orchestrator
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/running/pull/2741
- Simulation dashboard: https://dashboards.redwood.ai/d/priming/simulations

Risks / trade-offs:
- Aggressive priming increases cost and may temporarily inflate CPU/GPU usage. We mitigate with rate-limited shadow traffic and cost dashboards.
- Model-variant fallback introduces potential semantic drift. We'll tie fallback decisions to eval suites per-route and record fallbacks to notify product owners.
- Overly conservative quorum gating can increase time-to-failover; parameters must be tuned with chaos tests.

Overview

This document describes the canonical canary provisioning pipeline we use to introduce new GPU node pools and IaC changes into production. It combines Terraform module contracts, CI/CD promotion, automated smoke validation, and automated safety-net rollback to reduce blast radius when provisioning GPUs (spot or on-demand) across accounts and regions. The intended audience is infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners.

Goals

- Reduce risk of large-scale GPU provisioning incidents by phasing changes into small canaries.
- Provide automated safety nets (health gates, quota checks, cost caps) that fail fast.
- Maintain reproducible IaC artifacts and promote golden images with traceable provenance.
- Integrate with cost and quota tooling so provisioning respects budgets and SLAs.

Scope

Applies to: GPU node pools managed by our Terraform modules (gpu-node-pool), node bootstrap and golden-image pipelines, and CI/CD pipelines that run terraform apply in customer or infra accounts. Excluded: ephemeral CI-only pools created inside ephemeral test clusters.

Design overview

Runtime recovery patterns — API operator notes
STATUS: draft
Purpose:
This is a lightweight, operator-focused runbook for common API failure modes we see in the field: client-visible timeouts, elevated 429s (rate limiting/throttling), degraded streaming (chunked responses or stalled streams), and elevated error rates (5xx). The goal is to give on-call engineers quick, actionable patterns to recover service and gather diagnostics for a follow-up postmortem.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to Redwood hosted API endpoints and the gateway + serving runtime path.
- Assumes access to SRE dashboards, prometheus/grpc metrics, Kibana/Cloud logs, and K8s/infra execution privileges.
- Primary contact for infra actions: eng-sre oncall; escalate to serving-runtime team for model/runtime-specific behavior.

Severity rubric (quick reference):
- Sev-1: Global customer impact, >50% increase in latency or >10% 5xx across traffic for more than 5 minutes.
- Sev-2: Partial region or subset customers affected, degradations noticeable but not platform-wide.
- Sev-3: Small subset of requests or tail latencies affecting a small %; debugging/monitoring.

Detection — queries and alerts to check first:
- Prometheus (examples):
  - error rate: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job=\"api-gateway\",status=~\"5..\"}[1m])) by (route)
  - client timeouts: rate(api_client_timeouts_total[1m])
  - 429s: sum(rate(http_requests_total{status=\"429\"}[1m])) by (route)
  - streaming stalls: histogram_quantile(0.95, rate(stream_chunk_duration_seconds_bucket[2m])) > 5
- Kibana: search for 5xx spikes and correlated traces (trace_id present).
- Logs: look for repeated stack traces, OOMKilled, or connection refused from runtime.

Operator checklist (first 10 minutes):
1) Acknowledge alert in incident channel (SRE-ops on Slack), note start time, severity, any initial hypotheses.
2) Gather top-3 signals: 5xx rate, 429 rate, p95/p99 latency, error distribution by route/model/region.
3) If traffic is still flowing, switch non-critical traffic to fallback/legacy model (see routing fallbacks below).
4) If traffic is overwhelming gateway, enable traffic shaping or emergency rate-limit by route (gateway config) to preserve healthy backends.
5) Collect a minimal set of traces (one good, one failed) and share trace ids in channel.

--
A) Client-visible timeouts (external requests failing with 504/timeout)
- Quick checks:
  - Are downstream runtimes experiencing CPU or GPU contention? Check GPU util and host load.
  - Are we seeing long queue times in the gateway (request queue depth)?
  - Has a rollout just happened? (check recent rollouts/PRs)
- Immediate mitigations:
  - If queue depth high: temporarily reduce max-concurrency for expensive routes to allow short requests to proceed (gateway config).
  - If rollout suspect: roll back the last canary / pause rollout.
  - If runtime slow due to quantization/kernel issue: switch route to a known-stable model variant (e.g., quantized->fp16) via routing policy.
- Useful commands:
  - kubectl get pods -n serving -l app=runtime -o wide
  - kubectl top pod/rw-pod-123 -n serving
  - ssh to host -> nvidia-smi / dmesg | tail -n 50
--
B) Elevated 429s (rate limiting / throttling)
- Quick checks:
  - Is 429 coming from gateway (we're rejecting) or from downstream service (we're being rejected)? Check headers and gateway logs.
  - Did a traffic spike or bursty client start? Identify top IPs/keys.
- Immediate mitigations:
  - If gateway is the source: increase tenant burst windows or temporarily relax global rate limit for affected tier (short window) while monitoring cost.
  - If downstream service is rejecting: apply traffic split to a compatible fallback model endpoint or increase capacity (scale up serving pool).
  - Implement short-lived per-key throttles to protect platform: identify top offenders and throttle them more aggressively.
--
  - Kibana query: status:429 AND route:\"/v1/generate\" | top api_key
  - Redis rate limit counters: redis-cli -n 2 GET rate:api_key:abcd1234
  - Scale example: kubectl scale --replicas=8 deployment/runtime-pool-v1 -n serving
- Notes: avoid blanket removal of rate limits without a plan; document temporary exceptions in the incident channel with TTL.

C) Degraded streaming (partial chunks, long gaps between chunks)
- Quick checks:
  - Is the streaming proxy (gateway) reporting slow chunk delivery or lost TCP windows? Check network error counters.
  - Is the runtime returning data slowly (large token generation time)? Compare generate_token_latency_histogram by model.
- Immediate mitigations:
  - Fall back to short polling endpoints for critical customers while stream issue is mitigated.
  - If proxy memory or file descriptor limits are causing pauses, rotate proxy pods (kubectl rollout restart).
  - If it's model-level slowdown, route to a lower-latency variant or perform model warmup to rebuild KV caches.
- Commands and checks:
  - ss -tanp | grep :443 on gateway host to check connection states
  - kubectl logs gateway-abc -n gateway --tail=200 | grep chunked
  - curl -v --http1.1 https://api.redwood.ai/v1/stream?model=xyz and observe chunk timing
- Notes: collect a streaming trace (request id + timestamps of chunk events) for postmortem.

D) Elevated error rates (5xx spikes)
--
  - Route traffic away from failing pool: mark nodes unhealthy in service discovery or use routing filter to exclude pool.
  - If cause unknown and broad, serve degraded-but-safe responses (empty assistant reply with 200 + explain header) for a short time to preserve UX while investigating.
  - Engage the responsible owner and create a bug with priority to fix production cause.
- Commands/examples:
  - envoy stats, runtime endpoints: curl http://localhost:9901/stats | grep upstream_rq
  - Toggle route: POST /admin/v1/routes/<route>/override (internal admin API)
- Notes: collect core dumps/logs if suspect OOM or panic; preserve instance for SRE-debug.

Routing fallbacks and traffic shaping (common patterns):
- Canary rollback: if a canary is suspect, set canary weight to 0 and promote last stable.
- Traffic split example: route 90%->stable, 10%->canary; shift to 100/0 to stabilize.
- Emergency shaping: per-tenant token bucket reduction for 10 minutes with monitoring and automated rollback. Document TTL and reason.

Diagnostics & evidence to collect (minimum):
- Top-5 failing routes, top-10 affected customers (api_key or tenant), p95/p99 before and during incident, representative traces (one success, one failure), relevant pod logs/stack traces, GPU/host metrics if runtime involved, config snapshots (gateway and routing).

Escalation path and owners:
- Oncall SRE -> if runtime or model suspected -> notify serving-runtime team (pager), if networking -> infra-networking.
- Pager rotations and contact list are in Confluence (link in linked_artifacts). For Sev-1, call product + engineering leads and CS for customer comms.

Post-incident: short retrospective template (to be completed within 48h)
--
- What mitigations restored service
- Why existing controls did not prevent or detect earlier
- Action items (owner + due date) with severity and follow-up verification steps

Known caveats and gotchas (operator knowledge):
- Rolling restarts of gateway remove in-flight HTTP/1.1 streams; prefer connection draining when possible.
- GPU OOMs often look like service-level latency spikes; check host dmesg for Nvidia driver OOM messages rather than just app logs.
- Some SDK clients silently retry and amplify traffic (thundering herd) — identify client SDK versions in logs.
--

Appendix — quick command cheatsheet (copy-paste):
- kubectl get pods -n serving -l app=runtime -o wide
- kubectl logs <pod> -n serving --since=1h | tail -n 200
- kubectl top pod <pod> -n serving

Reliability Engineering makes Redwood Inference's customer-facing runtime predictably available, diagnosable, and safe to change. Cross-layer Observability & Diagnostics Playbook — Burst and Degradation Incidents
STATUS: published
Summary
-------
This playbook describes a cross-layer, repeatable approach for detecting, diagnosing, and mitigating short-duration bursts and progressive degradation in the Serving Runtime. It bridges runtime architecture, kernel scheduling signals, profiling playbooks, and benchmarking checks so oncall and runtime engineers can quickly restore SLOs and reduce mean time to innocence (MTTI).

Scope and audience
------------------
- Scope: Hosted + Dedicated runtime clusters and the operator-facing control-plane paths (Dispatcher, SlotAllocator, KernelRunner, KVCache, and Runtime Router).
- Audience: Serving runtime oncall, runtime engineers, release owners, and performance SREs.

Goals and SLO references
------------------------
- Primary detection SLOs: 95th token-latency < 100ms, 99th token-latency < 300ms for default small-model profile. (See per-model SLO sheet.)
- Operational goals: initial triage within 5 minutes, mitigation (fallback or ramp) within 15 minutes, restore to within 10% of baseline P95 within 60 minutes.

How this playbook fits with other docs
-------------------------------------
This is an operational layer that references: profiling playbooks for telemetry sampling, kernel-scheduler design docs for decision points, benchmarking suite for reproducible load, and existing runbooks for fallback and warmstart. Use this playbook when alerts indicate sudden tail-latency or progressive throughput drop.

Key concepts and system components
----------------------------------
--
- SlotAllocator: assigns execution slots (cohort/priority) used by the scheduler. Tracks queue lengths and admission metrics.
- KernelRunner: GPU process pool executing kernels. Emits kernel_latency_hist, kernel_qps, kernel_error_rate, and kernel_memory_pressure.
- KVCache: per-session prefix cache. Key signals: hit_rate, eviction_rate, and warmup_latency.
- Runtime Router / Graceful Fallback: orchestrates model variant fallbacks and cross-region routing.

Signal catalog and quick thresholds
----------------------------------
(Use these to prioritize initial checks.)

| Signal (metric)                      | Type         | Quick threshold (when to escalate) |
|--------------------------------------|--------------|------------------------------------|
| dispatch.request_p95_ms              | latency      | > baseline * 1.2 or > 200ms       |
| kernel_latency_p95_ms                | latency      | > 1.5x baseline                   |
--

Note: baseline is the rolling 7-day median for the service and model profile.

Triage checklist (first 5 minutes)
----------------------------------
1) Validate alert and scope
   - Confirm alert: check Alerting UI + trace sample in the last 2 minutes.
   - Determine scope: single node, single pool, entire region, or global. Use the Dispatcher topology view.
2) Quick telemetry pull
   - Pull P95/P99 for dispatch.*, kernel_*, kvcache.* and slot_allocator.* for last 30m vs 3h.
   - Commands (on the runbook box):
     ```bash
     rmetric query --service=dispatcher --metrics="dispatch.request_p95_ms,dispatch.request_p99_ms" --range=30m
     rmetric query --pool=kernerrunner --metrics="kernel_latency_p95_ms,kernel_queue_depth" --range=30m
--
   - Look for recent policy changes (priority weights, admission caps). If there was a rollout in the last hour, rollback to the previous scheduler config.
   - Check GPU mismatch signals: `rkctl node inspect --node <id>` -> note nvlink errors, thermal events.
B. Admission and backpressure
   - Validate admission thresholds: `SlotAllocator.admit_rate` vs observed arrival rate.
   - If admission is overly conservative, temporarily increase soft-cap by +10% and monitor.
   - If admission is broken, flip to the safe fallback profile: `rkctl route set-fallback --route <route> --profile reduced-memory`
C. KV cache warmup cascade
--
------------------------------------------------
- Short term (minutes): route to warm fallback model variant in-region; increase admission soft-cap by 5–10%; reduce batch size target to lower per-call kernel time.
- Medium term (hours): evict peaky low-util priority cohorts; initiate rolling restart of KernelRunner pool if drivers show instability; apply kernel restart mitigation which drains pending short calls first.
- Long term (post-incident): schedule simulation in the benchmarking suite to reproduce the burst, add synthetic traffic signature to the mixed-workload SLO test, and create a scheduler policy change with canary and rollout plan.

Diagnostic playbook for kernel-level regressions
------------------------------------------------
1) Reproduce with a targeted microbenchmark
   - Use the perf harness: `bench-run --profile kernel-latency --model <model> --sequence 256 --concurrency 8 --duration 5m`
   - Collect kernel traces: `kerntrace collect --pool <pool> --out /tmp/kerntrace.pb`
2) Compare kernel signature to baseline
   - Run diff against golden: `kerntrace diff /tmp/kerntrace.pb gs://benchmarks/kernel-gold/<model>.pb`
3) If reproducible, tag as kernel-regression and create a hotfix branch with kernel config rollback. Include the diff and perf artifacts in the PR.

Benchmarks and quick acceptance tests
------------------------------------
Use the standard benchmarking suite to validate mitigations before full rollout. Minimum test matrix:
- Mixed workload replay (30m): baseline QPS, 30% long sequences, 20% high-concurrency short sequences.
- Kernel microbench: 1–8 batch sizes, sequence 16/128/512.
- Admission and fallback test: inject synthetic saturating arrival and assert fallback triggers within 10s.
--
Sample benchmark run (CLI)
```bash
benchctl run --suite mixed-workload --tag incident-capture-$(date +%s) --params "qps=500,duration=30m,seqmix=0.3:512,0.5:128,0.2:16"
benchctl collect --artifact incident-capture-1234 --to gs://bench-results/incident-capture-1234
```

Release notes and change correlation
--
- Kernel memory fragmentation causing soft OOMs under interleaved batches (mitigation: apply compacting GC in 2.3.1-hotfix and restart KernelRunner).
- GRPC connection recycling leading to small head-of-line stalls at the Dispatcher (workaround: increase connection pool size temporarily).

Runbook appendices and artifacts to collect
-------------------------------------------
Collect these during the incident and attach to the postmortem:
- Top 20 traces (dispatch) during incident window.
- kernel_trace.pb files for affected KernelRunner nodes.
- SlotAllocator decision log for the interval.
- Bench artifacts if a reproduction was run (benchctl outputs).
- Release correlation snapshot (release-control export).

Post-incident actions (owner: runtime-performance squad)
-------------------------------------------------------
1) Assign postmortem owner within 24h.
2) Reproduce incident in bench lab with identical traffic signature within 72h.
3) Create follow-up tickets: scheduler policy change, kernel tuning, KVCache prefetch improvements, or infra remediation (if hardware).
4) Add a synthetic SLO probe to the mixed-workload suite for future detection.

Operational contacts and escalation
----------------------------------
- Oncall (runtime): #runtime-oncall Slack, Pager schedule in PagerDuty
- Kernel squadra: kern-team@redwood.com
- Infra hardware: infra-hw@redwood.com

Maintenance checklist (for release owners)
-----------------------------------------
- Before rolling scheduler changes: run the canary matrix (3% traffic) for 60 minutes against mixed workload.
- Attach bench artifacts and kernel diffs to the PR.
- Notify SRE and runtime performance reviewers 24h prior to rollout.

Revision history
----------------
--
-------------------------
- Dispatcher traces dashboard: /dashboards/dispatcher/traces
- Mixed-workload bench suite: /tools/benchctl/doc
- Scheduler policy language reference: confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles-2026
- Kernel tracing guide: confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/kernel-observability-sla-profiling-cadence-2024

If you have questions or need a walkthrough, ping the runtime-performance squad in #runtime-performance and request a live lab replication session.
